headings.title: Definition and Scale of HIV Orphans in Nigeria
headings.content: An **HIV orphan** is a child under the age of 18 who has lost one or both parents to an illness related to Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS). Nigeria carries one of the heaviest burdens of vulnerable children globally due to the HIV epidemic. When primary breadwinners succumb to the disease, families fracture, leaving extended relatives—often aging grandmothers—to shoulder the care of multiple children without adequate financial resources.

headings.title: Psychosocial and Emotional Vulnerabilities
headings.content: The psychological impact of losing parents to a stigmatized disease goes far beyond standard grief. Children often witness prolonged, painful illnesses and subsequent deaths, predisposing them to anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress. Chronic stress negatively alters childhood development. Isolation sets in quickly when peers withdraw due to community misconceptions about how the virus spreads.

headings.title: Physical Health and Nutritional Risks
headings.content: Orphaned children face immediate threats to basic survival needs. Food insecurity leads directly to malnutrition, stunting, and wasting. Without parental guidance and household income, access to clean water, routine immunizations, and prompt treatment for common ailments like malaria drops significantly. Furthermore, children born to HIV-positive mothers who missed prevention of mother-to-child transmission interventions may harbor undiagnosed perinatal infections.

headings.title: Stigma, Discrimination, and Human Rights
headings.content: Stigma related to HIV/AIDS stains the lives of surviving children. Communities sometimes associate the children with the disease, leading to social ostracism, bullying in schools, and denial of basic human rights. Property grabbing is another severe violation where deceased parents' lands and assets are seized by relatives, leaving the orphans completely destitute and vulnerable to exploitation.

headings.title: Community Health Nursing Assessment
headings.content: Community health nurses serve on the front lines of identifying vulnerable children. Assessment goes beyond physical vital signs to evaluate household stability, nutritional status using mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), immunization records, and school attendance. Nurses must screen for signs of depression, abuse, and neglect during home visits, collaborating with local leaders to map out families requiring urgent intervention.

headings.title: Support Systems and Caregiving Models
headings.content:
- **Kinship Care**: Extended family members take in the children, maintaining cultural roots and familial bonds.
- **Foster Care**: Non-relative families vetted by social welfare agencies provide temporary homes.
- **Child-Headed Households**: Older siblings assume parental roles due to a lack of adult relatives, facing extreme economic and psychological burdens.
- **Institutional Care**: Orphanages serve as a last resort when family-based care fails, though long-term institutionalization hampers social development.

headings.title: Policy Frameworks and Interventions in Nigeria
headings.content: Nigeria implements national action plans focused on orphans and vulnerable children (OVC). These policies aim to provide cash transfers, educational subsidies, and healthcare access. Non-governmental organizations work alongside community health structures to establish local safety nets. Nurses play a vital role in linking vulnerable households to these established social welfare programs and free treatment services.
